From St. Gallen to Tübingen

title: Childhood and youth in St. Gallen (1852–1871)
text:
Childhood and youth in St. Gallen (1852–1871)

The formative early years

Adolf Schlatter came from a long-established St. Gallen family whose roots can be traced back to the 15th century and which produced an unusually large number of Christian figures. His grandmother Anna Schlatter (1773–1826) was in close contact with leading men of the Awakening (such as Lavater, Jung-Stilling and Boos) and was distinguished by a remarkable ecumenical broad-mindedness: the eminent Catholic moral theologian and later Regensburg bishop Johann Michael Sailer regularly spent part of his holidays for a time, together with Catholic friends, in St. Gallen in order to cultivate spiritual fellowship with the Protestant Anna Schlatter and her sisters. Among her numerous descendants (she herself had 13 children), by the time of the Second World War there were six missionaries and 66 theologians alone. The two best known of them were Adolf Schlatter and his cousin Theodor Zahn (1838–1933), who, alongside his patristic studies, gained significance above all through his New Testament commentaries.

Adolf Schlatter was born on 16 August 1852 in St. Gallen as the seventh child of the merchant Stephan Schlatter. The down-to-earth biblical piety of his parental home, shaped by the Awakening, marked him deeply. As a man of over 70 he confessed: "From my parents I received the Bible, prayer, the Sunday, the clarification of what the words faith and love mean." His parents "lived before us and for us in bright light and … from the very beginning I saw how a life led before God unfolds. The power with which we children were embraced by our parents' faith was the precondition and root from which my own life story grew." The formative influence of the parental home can hardly be overestimated for an understanding of his theological development: here the spiritual foundations were laid to which he remained faithful — for all the later necessary demarcation, development and correction.

Two aspects deserve particular emphasis:

Schlatter's parents combined the seriousness of following Christ with joy in God's creation and redemption, so that the large brood of children (three boys and five girls) experienced being a Christian not as a burden but as a gift. Through their nature-loving way of life (hiking, getting to know the local flora and fauna) Schlatter became a great connoisseur and lover of nature. This joy in creation lastingly shaped his theological work and led to a pronounced affirmation of creation as well as to a special appreciation of nature as part of the divine glory.

No less far-reaching was the confessional separation of his parents — and the exemplary way in which they handled it: the father broke with the Reformed church, had himself re-baptised and in 1837 became a co-founder of a Baptist congregation in St. Gallen; the mother, for reasons of conscience, remained with the children in the established church. Despite the painful separation, the bond of the parents in faith and in love endured. For Schlatter's theological development this became a key experience: "The parents attained the fellowship of faith despite their ecclesial separation because their faith arose not from the church but from Jesus … Jesus was shown to me as the decisive ground of faith that determines everything." In the example of his parents the abiding distinction between personal faith (fides qua) and theological doctrine (fides quae) became clear to him — an experience that preserved him throughout his life from a narrow confessionalism.

Despite modest financial means, Schlatter was able to attend the municipal grammar school from 1865 to 1871 and stood out through outstanding achievements. Especially striking was his exceptional gift for languages, which moved one of his teachers, the later Basel professor of comparative linguistics Franz Misteli, to give him regular private lessons in Greek. Schlatter learned Latin and Greek, as well as French and — voluntarily — English and Hebrew. These years awakened in him the "scholarly will" and laid the foundation for that outstanding philological education which characterised his later exegetical work. His first encounter with theological liberalism and idealist philosophy did unsettle him, yet could not shake the biblical piety conveyed by his parents. For a short time he considered studying philology, until a remark by one of his sisters made him aware that his "no" to theology sprang from unbelief. The decision he then made for the study of theology he experienced as so irrevocable a taking-into-service for God that it took on for him the character of a "conversion".

title: Theological studies in Basel and Tübingen (1871–1875)
text:
Theological studies in Basel and Tübingen (1871–1875)

Academic grounding

In the summer semester of 1871 Schlatter began his theological studies in Basel. From the outset his studies were marked by an unreserved willingness to engage seriously with the questions of academic theology. In the second semester he fell into a grave crisis of faith which — at least for a moment — even led him to doubt the existence of God. In that crisis Schlatter had Luther's experience: "temptation teaches us to heed the Word" (Isa 28:19, unrevised Luther translation). Decisive for overcoming the crisis was not a sudden experience but the continuous engagement with Holy Scripture, which he did not interrupt even in his affliction.

During his four Basel semesters Schlatter's studies were remarkably broad: alongside the theological lectures he attended several philosophers (among them Friedrich Nietzsche), the historian Jakob Burckhardt and the Arabist Socin. At the centre of his philosophical studies stood the philosophy of the modern age, with particular attention to German idealism. The influence of idealism on theology and intellectual life was to occupy him for the rest of his life. The yield of the Basel period consisted above all in broad historical knowledge and the abiding insight into history as an essential dimension of human life and thought. None of the Basel philosophers and theologians, however, was able to exert a deeper influence on his theological convictions.

Only in his three Tübingen semesters (SS 1873 – SS 1874) did Schlatter meet a teacher whose personality and theology captivated him in equal measure. In the Swabian biblicist Johann Tobias Beck he found for the first time a professor of theology whose spiritual existence and scholarly work he experienced as an unaffected unity: "In the lecture hall he was confessor and researcher at once and made visible to us that he believed what he thought. Hence he spoke of God not as of one absent …" Many fellow students were fascinated by Beck's personal charisma and the pastoral urgency of his lectures; they were intellectually demanding and at the same time touched the conscience.

Schlatter was moreover deeply impressed by Beck's biblical theology. Beck convinced him both of the substantial reliability of Scripture as the foundation and norm of all theological thought and of the sustaining wholeness and unity that underlies the undeniable plurality of its statements. Schlatter was thereby prompted towards a theology of unity that overcomes false alternatives: in his exegesis he sought to bring out the inner unity of the New Testament canon despite the diversity of early Christian traditions; in his systematic theology he strove to show apparent opposites (e.g. revelation and reason, law and gospel, the grace and the wrath of God, justification and sanctification) in their complementary unity and so to avoid false alternatives.

For all these impulses, Schlatter did not become a "disciple" of Beck. His diligent study of Luther in Tübingen preserved him from adopting the un-Reformational, primarily effective version of Beck's doctrine of justification, which understood the righteousness of God imputed to the believer as a "new natural disposition". His particular gift for historical connections likewise kept him from taking over Beck's rather unhistorical approach. Thus he left Tübingen after three semesters rich in impulses but without having found a dogmatician who had "moved him with a strong hand …"

After a final semester in Basel he sat the theological examination in order to enter church service. Neither his outstanding examination result (top marks in all subjects) nor a tempting offer from Prof. Riggenbach to acquire the theological licentiate with the help of a generous scholarship could dissuade him from leaving scholarship behind in order to work as a pastor "with all earnestness and holy love, so that the Protestant gifts of salvation may be preserved for our people …" A strong longing for practical ministry had taken hold of him.

title: Pastor in Kilchberg, Neumünster and Keßwil (1875–1880)
text:
Pastor in Kilchberg, Neumünster and Keßwil (1875–1880)

Practical experience

The years as pastor in Kilchberg (1875), Neumünster (1875–1876) and Keßwil (1877–1880) were for Schlatter so fulfilling a time that, as a lecturer, he long felt a "strong longing for the pastorate". He came to know the bright and the shadowed sides of the situation of the established church. In Neumünster (Zurich) he encountered particularly difficult conditions marked by strong dechurching and moral decline.

During this time he gained the friendship of the pastor Edmund Fröhlich, who drew his attention to the Catholic philosopher Franz von Baader (1765–1841) and helped him to combine the pastorate with theological work. His intensive engagement with Baader shaped Schlatter's dogmatic and ethical thought, his epistemology and his assessment of idealism. In Baader he at last found a systematic thinker who "moved him with a strong hand". At the same time Schlatter retained reservations about Baader's speculative-theosophical orientation.

The three years in Keßwil above Lake Constance "filled themselves richly with what is lovely in the pastorate, with what gives it its spiritual depth, and with the natural happiness it grants us." Schlatter felt thoroughly at home there and came to know Susanna Schoop, whom he married in January 1878. Five children came from the marriage; she became for him a source of great strength for his theological and spiritual work.

title: Privatdozent in Bern (1880–1888)
text:
Privatdozent in Bern (1880–1888)

The beginning of his teaching career

Schlatter would probably have remained a pastor had not pietist circles in Bern asked him in 1880 to habilitate at the theological faculty as a Privatdozent, in order to represent a Scripture-bound theology over against liberalism and mediating theology. Although giving up the pastorate meant a great sacrifice, he agreed. Despite considerable resistance the habilitation succeeded by regular means; in January 1881 he began his academic teaching.

The start was not easy: liberal colleagues kept their distance because of his "Bible faith"; among some of his supporters an alleged lack of fidelity to the Bible aroused mistrust. Schlatter sought to counter both by combining an unprejudiced, observing interpretation of Scripture ("nothing but the truthful carrying-out of observation") with a credible submission to the authority of Scripture — a hallmark of his theology.

His Bern lectures covered an unusual thematic breadth: Old and New Testament, church-historical, systematic and philosophical subjects. He thereby laid the foundation for the later breadth of his teaching (NT in Greifswald and Tübingen, systematics in Berlin). In substance he unfolds a concept of empirical theology grounded in the observation of experienceable reality (history and creation). The aim was a Christocentric, biblically founded, ecclesially responsible alternative to the liberal understanding of theology — without adopting the narrowings of some "positive" theology.

In 1885 his prize-winning study Der Glaube im Neuen Testament appeared, which won him scholarly recognition at a stroke. Several universities sought him; in 1888 he accepted a call to Greifswald in order to improve his working conditions and ecclesial influence.

title: Professor of New Testament in Greifswald (1888–1893)
text:
Professor of New Testament in Greifswald (1888–1893)

First professorship

The years in the Baltic city of Greifswald were marked by a fruitful working partnership with the Lutheran systematician Hermann Cremer (1834–1903) — bound, despite differing formations, by friendship and spiritual understanding. Both advocated a theology that has reverence for Scripture as its foundation and wards off any "mastery of the theologian that exalts itself above Scripture".

Together they sought a scholarly defensible alternative to the liberal theology of the Ritschl school. Under its two most distinguished representatives, the "Greifswald school" brought the faculty to a high point and attracted many students. Here Schlatter lectured for the first time on dogmatics (1892/93) and gained in Wilhelm Lütgert (1863–1938) a gifted pupil who independently carried important impulses further.

title: Professor of Systematic Theology in Berlin (1893–1898)
text:
Professor of Systematic Theology in Berlin (1893–1898)

Systematic development

In 1893 Schlatter followed the call to Berlin, where a professorship was established as a counterweight to the prevailing liberal theology. Despite initial resistance, a friendly relationship developed with Adolf von Harnack — amid open theological differences. When Harnack said, "The only thing that separates me from my colleague Schlatter is the question of miracles!", Schlatter interjected: "No, the question of God!" On Schlatter's departure in 1898 Harnack confessed: "I miss you … and feel it as a gap …"

In Berlin Schlatter taught systematic theology and, for the first time, Christian ethics (1894). His lectures probed the "front line of secular thought" and wrestled for a dogmatically, ethically and philosophically defensible Christian alternative.

In 1897, together with Hermann Cremer, he founded the journal Beiträge zur Förderung christlicher Theologie. It was not a party organ but was meant to serve the church and to advance a theology that develops and purifies knowledge beyond the existing stock. Already the first issue, with Der Dienst des Christen, showed programmatically the deficits of post-Reformation orthodoxy (among others love, sanctification, mission, the laity), which are rooted in part in narrowings of Reformation theology — a thesis that Schlatter later substantiated further.

The aim was a "renewed, deepened reading of Scripture" that appropriates the "whole content of Scripture" — not for mere restoration but for the expansion and correction of the inheritance. For Schlatter this was a "completion of the Reformation". Towards the end of the Berlin period he accepted the call to Tübingen: he expected "home" rather than a metropolis, "hills, fields and woods" — and a lecture hall that allows for fruitful exchange.

title: The height of his activity in Tübingen (1898–1938)
text:
The height of his activity in Tübingen (1898–1938)

Four decades of formative work

In Tübingen Schlatter spent the last forty years of his life and experienced the height of his teaching. At first Württemberg students met him with reserve, but interest soon grew strongly — later as many as 600 listeners attended his lectures.

A deep turning point was the early death of his wife (1907). As never before, Schlatter saw himself placed before eternity and gained the impression that he should "finish what has been begun." In the following seven years he summed up the previous yield of his work in four great volumes: the two-volume Neutestamentliche Theologie (Das Wort Jesu, Die Lehre der Apostel) as well as Das christliche Dogma and Die christliche Ethik.

His dogmatics combined biblical truth and knowledge of reality in an independent way and continues to have a profound effect to this day. Paul Schneider, who suffered martyrdom in 1939, experienced a theological turn under its influence. Schlatter's ethics was still being recommended decades later for its modernity.

In 1915 Schlatter completed the summation of his life's work with a metaphysics that sets out his basic philosophical convictions. Despite the urging of Wilhelm Lütgert he did not publish the work; it appeared only in 1987. The background was the escalation of the First World War, to which his son Paul had already fallen victim in 1914. Deeply grieved, he wrote: "… loneliness, the pressure of war, …, the memory of the uncounted … lies paralysing upon me … The future lies in darkness … For me it is autumn …" At the same time he held fast: "We are led … by the gracious hand of the good Shepherd …"

After the outbreak of war, Schlatter concentrated in his teaching entirely on the exegesis of the New Testament. His aim was a rigorous observation of the text that thinks history and pneumatology together. What was fascinating was that for him exegesis was not only philology but theology — bound up with pastoral care for students (office hours, "Open Evenings").

The development of systematic theology in the interwar period was shaped by dialectical theology. Schlatter shared some of its criticisms (e.g. of anthropocentrism) but also saw troubling reductions (creation, nature, history; a curtailment of the testimony of Scripture; the detachment of faith from reason).

In 1930 — in his 78th year — Schlatter ended his academic teaching after more than 100 semesters. He used the remaining time for the nine volumes of the Erläuterungen zum Neuen Testament — the "harvest" of his lifelong exegesis.

He followed the rise of National Socialism with great concern. As early as 1931 he thought that the church could expect from National Socialism "at best benevolent tolerance"; in 1933 he foresaw a "path of grievous suffering". He rejected racial ideology and racial laws as well as the euthanasia programme. His last great work, the devotional book Kennen wir Jesus?, arose out of concern for the path of the German people.

When Schlatter died in 1938, many honoured him not only as a "teacher of the church" but as a "father in Christ". Friedrich von Bodelschwingh the Younger said: "… a leader to Christ … From this grave we take with us the charge to see to it that what Adolf Schlatter had to say to the church comes to new fruitfulness and abiding effect."

title: Theological interpretation as the goal of historical exegesis
text:
Theological interpretation as the goal of historical exegesis

Methodological grounding

Already in his Bern period Adolf Schlatter was concerned to practise an exegesis that does justice to the humanly historical and divinely pneumatic double character of Scripture. He recognised the legitimacy of historical method in principle — provided it is not distorted by ideological prior decisions (e.g. a Hegelian understanding of history, a rationalist understanding of reality). For him, historical research is constructive only in the service of theological interpretation. Contemporary exegesis, he held, often suffers from the fact that "historicism has swallowed up theology". An exclusively historical-critical exegesis therefore easily has a "chilling, paralysing" or even "destroying" effect, because it prevents the genuine encounter with Scripture.

His great works serve the twofold goal of historical and theological interpretation: the monograph Der Glaube im Neuen Testament (1885), which — according to Peter Stuhlmacher — remains to this day "unsurpassed" in "systematic coherence and historical precision"; further the two-volume Theologie des Neuen Testaments (1909/10), which brings out not only the differences but the theological unity of the New Testament traditions; as well as the popular Erläuterungen zum Neuen Testament (1887–1910) and the nine commentaries (among them Matthäus 1929, Markus 1935, Lukas 1931, Johannes 1930, Römer 1935, Korinther 1934, Pastoralbriefe 1936, 1. Petrus 1937, Jakobus 1932), some of which rank among the best of the 20th century.

title: Rabbinic Judaism as the horizon for understanding the New Testament
text:
Rabbinic Judaism as the horizon for understanding the New Testament

Contextual exegesis

When Schlatter began his teaching, knowledge of rabbinic Judaism in New Testament scholarship was slight: the Talmudic literature was widely ignored and reliance was placed almost solely on sources preserved in Greek. Schlatter gained early the conviction that the world of thought of the New Testament can be adequately understood only against the background of Palestinian Judaism — an insight that was then widely unfamiliar.

In the following decades he published numerous studies on the Judaism of the New Testament period and became one of the "foremost authorities" in this field. Historically outstanding is his comprehensive account Geschichte Israels von Alexander dem Großen bis Hadrian (1899), which describes "the ground" "on which Jesus and his own carried out their ministry" and soberly reflects on the ecclesial guilt towards Israel. Groundbreaking too are his studies on Josephus (among them Die Theologie des Judentums nach dem Bericht des Josefus), the fruit of decades of work — Schlatter is regarded as probably the finest Josephus scholar of his time.

These specialised studies lastingly shaped his exegesis: like scarcely anyone else he drew on contemporary Jewish sources in his commentaries. His guiding thesis — that the NT cannot be adequately interpreted historically without knowledge of Pharisaic and rabbinic Judaism — is today widely accepted.

title: Dogmatics as biblical-empirical theology
text:
Dogmatics as biblical-empirical theology

Systematic grounding

Schlatter's dogmatics was felt to be modern, even though in its results it was decidedly biblical and thus "conservative". Methodologically he ventured a comprehensive unfolding of his observing/empirical theology: like every science, theology too is to ground its claim to truth in the "facts" of salvation history and of creation. Schlatter is convinced that the truth of Scripture is confirmed in observable reality and need not merely be asserted.

Theologically this is grounded in the revelatio generalis (Rom 1:19f; 2:14f): God's revelation embraces "all that exists". Dogmatics is therefore not only a service to those who already believe but also a conversation with non-Christians. Accordingly Schlatter shows — disconcertingly for some — that human thought and life presuppose God's reality. He does not shrink from examining the classical arguments for God in order to make visible the adequate interpretation of reality by the biblical message.

title: Concrete ethics as the goal of theology
text:
Concrete ethics as the goal of theology

Practical dimension

In Schlatter's conviction, ethics is "theology arrived at its goal". In it, it becomes evident whether theology reaches the goal set by the Bible. Therefore the truth of Christianity is measured "always, perhaps predominantly, by its ethics". Mission and evangelisation succeed only if church and theology arrive at a "capable ethics".

Schlatter's Ethik (1914) impresses through its concreteness and closeness to life: as in the dogmatics, he combines biblical insight with an unprejudiced perception of the real. Christian ethics must not confine itself to an abstract description of the ethos or to mere formal determinations; as a "science turned towards the present" it asks how we, in our situation, fulfil the divine will that applies to us.

This means no relativisation of universally valid norms: both biblically ("God's commandments") and anthropologically (the creaturely constancy of the human being) there are abiding standards. Schlatter's pronounced theology of creation guards against a situation-ethical relativism: with creation there are given orders of creation, or a moral law directed towards justice and love as an expression of the Creator's will, which limit human freedom. Therefore he affirms — against the trend — a limiting natural law.

At the same time he does not deny the material distinctiveness of Christian ethics: methodologically it proceeds from the analysis of reality, but illuminates it in the light of the revelation of Christ and the apostolic testimony (with dense NT support). Thus empirical observation and Bible, nature and grace, creation and redemption all come equally into play. Christian ethics is a Christocentric and pneumatic ethics of love grounded in the gift of redemption.

title: Theology as service to the believing congregation
text:
Theology as service to the believing congregation

Ecclesial dimension

From the outset Schlatter understood his theological work as service to the believing congregation. Theology misses its goal when it is pursued for its own sake and loses sight of the needs of the congregations. He therefore deliberately devoted a considerable part of his output to the congregation.

Worth highlighting are — besides the Erläuterungen zum Neuen Testament — the popular Einleitung in die Bibel (1889), volumes of sermons (Der Ruf Jesu, Ich will ihn loben bis zum Tode and others), devotional books (Andachten, Kennen wir Jesus?) and collections of essays on fundamental questions of faith (Hülfe in Bibelnot, Gesunde Lehre and others).

His orientation to the congregation also shaped his activity and way of life: chairman of the Tübingen YMCA (1914–1918), preacher at the Stiftskirche, expositor in men's, women's and girls' groups. Thus — especially in Tübingen — he helped to reduce noticeably the gulf between academic theology and the congregation.

title: Theology as ecumenical service to the whole body of Christ
text:
Theology as ecumenical service to the whole body of Christ

Ecumenical vision

Schlatter's theology is distinguished by a remarkable ecumenical breadth. Through the confessional difference of his parents he came to know Reformed and free-church (Baptist) formations early; later the Catholic philosopher Franz von Baader and the Lutheran theologian Hermann Cremer were added. He was ready to receive what is in accord with Scripture from different traditions — without conversion.

This openness shaped his work and teaching. As a Protestant theologian committed to the Reformation inheritance, he understood his work as service to the whole body of Christ. The aim was to overcome the rift between the Protestant and Catholic churches. Early on he said: "The division of the church should be treated as that which must be overcome … Only then is the confessional character of theology legitimate" — without calling into question the right of the Reformation.

The inner obligation to ecumenical openness grows out of the binding to Scripture: the truth of the New Testament surpasses all confessional positions; therefore all churches are called to the purification and completion of their knowledge of the truth.

title: Philosophy as consistent realism
text:
Philosophy as consistent realism

Basic philosophical stance

Throughout his life Schlatter engaged intensively with philosophy, because it is of fundamental importance for theology: "The theologian always owes the philosophical movement serious critical attention …". This shapes his systematic works; it is especially visible in the lecture Die philosophische Arbeit seit Cartesius (1905/06) and in the metaphysics written in 1915.

Starting from the conviction that the "redemption granted" through Jesus is also a redemption to objectivity and thus to the possibility of the "act of seeing", Schlatter devised a philosophical realism: an understanding of reality that does justice to the basic structures of the real — the world as the contingent creation of God, mutually underivable levels of being (nature and spirit), the human being as a personal being. The aim was to make the biblical understanding of reality plausible in philosophical categories.

In this the independence of philosophy is preserved; at the same time the history of philosophy shows the danger of ideological curtailments. In critical give and take, theology can help philosophy not to miss an ideology-free realism. Schlatter shares the insight (with P. Brunner) that the rationality of reason is threatened without the Christian faith.

A lasting influence on the theology of the 20th century

title: Reception and after-effect
text:
Reception and after-effect

Influence and international resonance

Because of its independence and versatility, Schlatter's life work resists any simple classification. His impulses had an effect in almost every area of theology — often beyond the customary polarisations and increasingly also internationally. Even theologians who went other ways took up essential impulses from his work. Remarkable is his continuing presence on the book market (over 30 titles), despite a language, method and content often felt to be demanding.

Undisputed today is his significance as a New Testament scholar and pioneer of the study of NT-era Judaism. Renowned exegetes took up his impulses and carried them further, among them Otto Michel, Karl-Heinrich Rengstorf, Julius Schniewind, Leonhard Goppelt, Martin Hengel and Peter Stuhlmacher.

As a systematician Schlatter found wide attention; with the rise of dialectical theology, however, his influence receded into the background. He demonstrably shaped or influenced significant systematicians (e.g. Wilhelm Lütgert, Hans Emil Weber, Paul Althaus; further Friedrich Brunstäd, Dietrich Bonhoeffer, Emil Brunner, Adolf Köberle, Wolfgang Trillhaas and later Klaus Bockmühl).

He also had an effect in other disciplines: among church historians (Karl Holl, Heinrich Bornkamm), practical theologians (Renatus Hupfeld, Karl Fezer), in mission theology (Wilhelm Oehler) and among church leaders (F. v. Bodelschwingh the Younger, Theophil Wurm, Kurt Scharf).

More recent research — drawing on the long-neglected literary estate — confirms his abiding significance. Johannes von Lüpke concludes: "It may well be time to return to Schlatter's theology in order to make progress in the current discussions." And Wilfried Härle: "In Schlatter there is a whole series of approaches to thought that I consider stimulating and forward-looking …" — an assessment that joins with Franz Mußner's words: "Schlatter's voice must not fall silent in the church."
